topic: Sneezing: reflex, heart myth, droplet distance, photic sneeze, holding it in
hook: What happens to your body when you sneeze

slides.title: It starts in your nose
slides.body: Irritants hit nerve endings in your nose. A signal races to your brainstem, which fires the sneeze reflex.
slides.image_prompt: Glowing pollen grains drifting toward a dark nasal-shaped tunnel, tiny electric sparks along nerve-like threads, dramatic macro lighting

slides.title: Your heart doesn't stop
slides.body: Pure myth. Chest pressure can briefly change your heart rhythm, but your heart keeps beating the whole time.
slides.image_prompt: Anatomical heart model on a dark table with a steady glowing pulse line wrapping around it, moody lighting

slides.title: The cloud travels far
slides.body: MIT researchers filmed sneeze clouds carrying droplets up to 8 meters across a room.
slides.image_prompt: Fine mist cloud of droplets expanding across a dark room, backlit so every droplet glows, long perspective

slides.title: Bright light can trigger it
slides.body: The photic sneeze reflex makes roughly 1 in 4 people sneeze when they step into bright sunlight.
slides.image_prompt: Blinding sunburst breaking through a dark doorway, sharp light rays and dust particles floating in the beam

slides.title: Never hold one in
slides.body: In 2018, doctors reported a man who tore his throat holding in a sneeze with his nose and mouth shut.
slides.image_prompt: A pressure gauge needle pushed into the red zone beside a cracked glass tube, dark dramatic background

cta: Follow so you never miss the next one
caption:
A sneeze is a reflex your brainstem fires. MIT researchers filmed sneeze clouds carrying droplets up to 8 meters across a room.

And holding one in is a bad idea. In 2018, doctors in the UK described a man who tore his throat after pinching his nose and closing his mouth mid-sneeze (BMJ Case Reports).

Be honest: do you sneeze when you look at the sun? 👇
